messages.body_plain:
Hi Edy,

On Tue, Dec 10, 2013 at 6:15 AM, Edy Coelho <edyceli...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hello Phil!
>
> I am using the difference of parameters and analysis of AIC, BIC and logLink to examine the dimension of the adjustment of the MIRT models.
>
> I've seen reports of Df and df.
>
> In my analysis I have 443 respondents and 32 questions for the exam in 2PL    mod1 <- mirt(dado,1, itemtype="2PL"):
> DF = 372
>
> How is the command DF and df?
>
> The amounts of the parameters df = 64 (ltm) in 2PL
>
> The estimated parameters would be 96  (n+n*m)  then df = r - m-1, df = 443-96-1, then
> df = 353?

Why would there by 96 parameters estimated? There are 32 slopes, and 32 intercepts, and in this model the latent mean and variance and constrained to be a standard normal. Otherwise, 443-64-1 = 378 is only the maximum possible number of df in the dataset.....if there are repeated response patterns, than the effective sample size drops from 443 to something smaller due to repetition.

That being said, the total df are no longer calculated in this way. Instead, the following form is used on the latest CRAN and dev versions:

df = prod(K) - #estimated.parameters - 1,

where K is a vector containing the number of unique responses for each item. This change doesn't affect nested model comparisons (it's really just adding a constant, so nested inferences don't change), but it will affect the G^2 model fit statistic. However, that is rarely printed now anyway due to common model spareness. Hope that helps.

Phil

messages.subject: Re: DF and df
messages.body_plain:
Hi Edy,

As I mentioned in an earlier message, the df are now calculated slightly differently in the models so negative df really can't happen any more in the nested model comparisons. You'll notice that nested model comparisons return the same results though (give or take, the newer versions use a smaller tolerance for convergence, which explains the difference in X2 and other values based on the log-likelihood), and that the difference between models has the same df for the approximate chi-square test. As it turns out the current version uses the more appropriate method for determining total df, so I would tend to use that instead. Hope that clarifies the issue.

Phil

Hi Hans,

I see your point about wanting to keep one groups as a kind of population model based on previous results while freely estimating the second group parameters. It's not the typical DIF approach, but if you have a good reason to do it this way then I see no real harm.

The first step I would do in this situation is to set up a highly constrained model, where across all groups you set the parameters equal to the population values you have while freely estimating the latent mean and variance. If no DIF exists, this will provide an unbiased estimate of group differences.

When testing DIF in this situation, it's perfectly fine to free the parameters in the second group only and test whether the log-likelihood significantly decreases via anova(), and simply loop over each item to run the tests. In fact, you could freely estimate *all* of the parameters in your focal group and compare the log-likelihood/information statistic (I would use information) drop to see if the included flexibility contributes to the overall model fit if you wanted to. If it does, DIF likely exists somewhere, and using item plots will help to see what exactly is happening.

It's too bad you want to treat your reference group as a population model, since there is a new DIF function specifically for running these kinds of analyses when multiple group samples are drawn. Could have made the looping a little easier, IMO. Cheers.

Phil

Correct, the model will still be identified (up to two parameters have to remain fixed actually for identification, but the rest are fair game).

As it turns out though if you are only keeping the reference group in with fixed parameters and latent N(0,1) distribution then you actually can do this without MG analysis at all. Since there are no equality constraints across groups, and the reference group never changes, the log-likelihoods across groups are strictly additive and therefore the non-estimated groups just serve to add a constant to the likelihood. Inference wouldn't change since strictly independent groups provide no additional information about the focal (sample, in this case) group. The multipleGroup function is really only good when you have two samples to compare, not in the case where you are comparing how one sample matches with population coefficients. Sorry for not recognizing that earlier.

Just set up your tests with a single group run using only your sample with the population coefficients you know, and perform likelihood-ratio tests on the less restricted versions of this model. If you are still interested in the latent mean and variance then try to set a slope coefficient to 1 and intercept parameter to 0 (match it with the population, as close as possible) so that the model is identified when these parameters are estimated.

are the error bars, which makes them doublely imprecise and hard to
interpret.

Typically these empirical estimates are used to visibly measure
goodness of fit, but with smaller sample sizes they don't perform well
at all (and with larger sample sizes there are better stats anyway,
like the S-X2). I certainly could add the error bars in to the plots,
I just wonder how useful they really are and whether over-plotting
will be an issue.

If you are only interested in how the parameter shapes might vary, I
think the more natural way to look at how the parameter space is
influenced by the model information. Check out the itemplot(mod, 1, CE
= TRUE) plot to generate confidence ellipses in parameter space that
are mapped into data-space (requires an information matrix to be
computed beforehand). This should get at the same idea as the error
bars in the plots you are looking for, though personally I think they
are a bit nicer and easier to grasp. Cheers.

Phil

On Sat, Dec 21, 2013 at 10:35 AM,  <bea...@gmx.de> wrote:
> ok, i reread about the estimation and mirt probably uses marginal maximum likelihood, right?

Correct. The latent scores aren't estimated during estimation since
they are integrated over instead. Hence obtaining factor score
estimates is really a secondary thing, in the same way as traditional
factor analysis or SEM.

>
> what about the distribution of ability, which is used in this approach? is this N(0,1) or the distribution of sum scores? Can one pass a distribution to the model estimation?

Yes you can! As of the latest CRAN version (1.1) you can specify your
own function to determine the latent densities for the theta
integration grid. The default is (multivariate) Gaussian, or when
estimating via empirical histograms the latent distribution is
determined empirically.

>
> and, finally: i read in Millsap "statistical approaches to measurement invariance" that there is a method, where the model is reestimated, given a vector of thetas. is something like this possible in mirt?

I've never tried this approach, but the package certainly has the
tools to do it (the MHRM algorithm sounds very similar, so it wouldn't
take much to make it accommodate it). I don't have the book to know
the specifics, so I'll have to look for it sometime after the
holidays. Cheers.

Phil
